job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Amira Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied computer science at Edinburgh and since September I've been a test engineer on a payments team at a bank. I write automated checks that make sure a payment screen still works after every change, and I spend a good part of the day working out why a test failed. I share a flat in Leith with my cousin Noor, and on Saturdays I help my dad in his phone repair shop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding the bug nobody else spotted, it feels like detective work. What wears me out is the meetings, and the fact that my manager keeps saying the team is 'lean', which I've learned means no new hires. I owe about 17,000 and I keep roughly six weeks of spending in my account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what a sensible person expected. I use an AI chat tool now and then to write a first draft of a test, and it saves maybe an hour a week. If that's all it is, I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved but not complacent. Test engineering is the sort of job that's part routine, so I'd still keep an eye on it. The bank is stable, my pay is typical, and my dad's shop is a backup if things get tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, ask my manager about moving from testing towards developing in a year or two, and put 150 a month on the loan. I'd also finish a cloud certificate, because it's cheap and looks good. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's my normal week with a bit of a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you less calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bank does another round of cuts most years in some department. They call it restructuring, and we've had one since I started. It wasn't my team, but I noticed who stopped coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you do when you noticed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I kept my head down and learned one more thing that week. It's not heroic, but it's what I do.

say: I'd say it's what a **sensible person** expected, and I'm happy with a small saving of time.
I'd tell my manager I'd like to move towards **development** within two years.
think: Privately I'm relieved but not complacent, because testing is partly **routine work**.
My dad's phone **repair shop** is a backup if money gets tight.
do: Finish a **cloud certificate** and ask about moving into development.
Put **150 a month** on the loan and keep my head down at restructuring time.
feel: **Calm**, really; it's my normal week with a bit of a safety net.
S0.quote: The bank does another round of cuts most years in some department.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on a **stable employer** and her father's shop, and she still watches restructuring closely.
Her habit is steady and practical: learn one more thing, don't make noise.
Say and think agree; the unspoken risk is the routine side of testing.

steps.text: Finish the cloud certificate by spring
Ask my manager about moving into development within two years
Pay 150 a month towards the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where you either learn it or get squeezed. At my bank, writing and checking test cases is already half automated, so I'd tell friends to use the tools properly and not just for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. Testing is a checking job and checking is exactly what the card names. The bank might need half as many testers, and the junior ones are usually first. My degree is good and my grades were good, but the bank doesn't hire on grades when software is cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who knows how to check the AI's tests. I'd use it daily instead of occasionally and start a log of where it gets things wrong. I'd also ask to join the new platform team, because that's where the hiring will be, and keep up my cloud certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep my head up. It's like waiting on exam results where you already did most of the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the log of mistakes do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's proof that someone needs to check the machine. If I can show my manager forty cases where it passed a bad payment screen, I'm useful. If I can't, I'm just a cheaper option for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another bank if yours cut testers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd already have a list of five firms in Edinburgh. I've kept in touch with two people from my internship, which my dad told me to do. He says in the shop, the customer you remember is the customer who comes back.

say: I'd say you either **squeezed**, so use the tools properly.
I'd tell friends **not to rely** on grades alone.
think: Testing is a checking job, and **checking** is exactly what the card names.
The bank might need **half as many testers**, and juniors are usually first.
do: Use the AI daily and keep a **log of its mistakes** to show my manager.
Ask to join the new **platform team**, where hiring will be.
feel: **Anxious**, but I'd keep my head up, like waiting for exam results.
S1.quote: If I can show my manager forty cases where it passed a bad payment screen, I'm useful.
fieldNote: She converts fear into **evidence**: a log that proves why a person still checks the machine.
Her father's shop lesson, about being remembered, shapes how she keeps **internship contacts** alive.
She is quietly realistic that good grades won't be enough.

steps.text: Use the AI tool daily and log every mistake it makes
Ask to join the new platform team
Message two internship contacts about openings in Edinburgh
Keep the cloud certificate on track

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for anyone to handle, and I'd want government and the big firms to say what they plan. I'd write to my MP because I can't think of anything better to do. I wouldn't post anything angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm alarmed. If AI can do almost any thinking job, testing goes first, and the bank cuts whole teams. By 2028 I'll be 24, with a loan and maybe six months of savings if I cut everything. The three extra years for robots won't help me, because I don't have a hands-on skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at my dad's shop on weekends to learn real repair skills, because phones still need hands. I'd cut spending to the bone and move back into my parents' house for a year to save rent. I'd also ask the bank, in writing, what its plan is for staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Quite a lot of 3 a.m. thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why repair skills and not a retraining course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because courses would be full of people doing the same thing, and an AI can teach the course too. A repair shop has a counter and a customer and a bit of trust. That's what a person has that a machine doesn't, at least until the robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be proud, I think, and wary. He's run that shop for nineteen years and he's seen the customers change, so he'd say don't put your whole life in it, but he'd teach me.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and I'd write to my MP.
I'd ask the bank for its **plan for staff** in writing.
think: If AI does almost any thinking job, **testing goes first** and the bank cuts whole teams.
I have no **hands-on skill** to fall back on.
do: Work weekends in my dad's **repair shop** to learn real repair skills.
Move back to my parents' house for a year to save **rent**.
feel: **Alarmed**; there'd be a lot of 3 a.m. thinking.
S2.quote: A repair shop has a counter and a customer and a bit of trust.
fieldNote: She grounds her plan in her **father's shop**, valuing trust and a counter over courses.
She admits she lacks a hands-on skill, which is why the **robot delay** doesn't comfort her.
Her say is calm and civic; her private fear is much sharper.

steps.text: Work Saturdays and Sundays in my dad's phone repair shop
Move back into my parents' house for a year
Cut spending to the bone and keep six months in the account
Write to my MP about the pace of change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if employers are honest. I'd tell Noor and my friends to start side projects now, and I'd ask for a mentor at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious but more focused. By 2031 I'll be 27, which is old enough to have a real position, and young enough to start over. The thinking work goes in 2031 but the hands-on side in 2034, so I think there's a window to move towards something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from testing to development in the next two years, get my cloud certificate, and then aim at security, because someone has to be accountable. I'd save 300 a month for a house deposit, and I'd keep weekends in the shop in case. I'd also keep using AI at work in the way that makes me useful, not just fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like a plan I could write on a whiteboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why security?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Banks need a person to be blamed when something goes wrong. I know that sounds cynical, but a regulator wants a name, not an algorithm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that your reason, or is there another?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's also the part I enjoy, hunting for the thing that doesn't fit. I'd choose it even if the money were the same.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan** if employers are honest.
I'd tell my cousin and friends to start **side projects** now.
think: By 2031 I'll be 27, old enough for a position and young enough to **start over**.
There's a window to move towards work with **people in it**.
do: Move from testing to **development**, then aim at security within five years.
Save **300 a month** for a deposit and keep helping in the shop.
feel: **Anxious**, but it feels like a plan I could write on a whiteboard.
S3.quote: Banks need a person to be blamed when something goes wrong.
fieldNote: She picks security for two reasons: **accountability** and the fact that she enjoys it.
She is anxious but sees a **whiteboard plan**, which matches her steady style.
Honest about the cynical reason; this is a person who names her own motives.

steps.text: Move from testing into development within two years
Aim for a security role by 2031
Save 300 a month for a house deposit
Keep working Saturdays in my dad's shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people use it. I'd say start now, learn the tools, and keep a skill with your hands too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy but fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, with registration or a master's, and a better sense of where I want to be. The AI would arrive into a life I've had time to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time master's in security or data after two years of working, save a deposit, and carry on learning new tools as they come. I'd also stay in touch with the shop, because it's the best proof my dad's advice works. I'd pay down the loan well before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. Ten years feels like a normal chunk of life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest thing that could go wrong in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I assume I have time and I stop learning. I'd relax for five years, then wake up in 2033 and realise I'm behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you guard against that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By setting a reminder every six months to check what's changed. It sounds silly, but I've kept a similar one for my passport since I was sixteen.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** if people start now.
I'd advise friends to learn the tools and keep a **hands-on skill**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 and the AI would arrive into a **life I've built**.
The danger is that I **relax** and wake up behind.
do: Study a part-time **master's** in security or data after two years of work.
Set a **six-month reminder** to check what has changed and pay down the loan.
feel: **Uneasy**, but not scared; ten years feels like a normal chunk of life.
S4.quote: I'd relax for five years, then wake up in 2033 and realise I'm behind.
fieldNote: Her risk in the long scenario is **complacency**, not job loss, a quietly sophisticated view.
She uses small **habits**, such as a six-monthly reminder, to guard against drift.
Mood stays uneasy because the loan and a lean team remain.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in security or data after two years
Pay the student loan off well before 2036
Set a reminder every six months to review what's changed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, because there'd be no time to build skills, and the bank could cut a whole team at once. What would help is honesty from my employer, a way to learn something practical, and a savings cushion. A bit of family backing helps too, and I'm lucky to have it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I've sounded calmer than I feel in the fast ones. I'd like it written down that being practical isn't the same as being unafraid.

headlineQuote: I'd like it written down that being practical isn't the same as being unafraid.
portrait: Amira is a 22-year-old **computer science graduate** testing a bank's payments software, owing about 17,000.
She is steady, uses an **AI tool** now and then, and builds proof of her value.
Her centre outlook shows in balanced answers and a readiness to lean on **family**, including her father's shop.
She is calm at the plateau, anxious when testing looks exposed, **alarmed** at two years and uneasy at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because there'd be no time to build skills before the bank cuts a whole team.
whatWouldHelp: **Honesty** from her employer, a practical way to learn something new, and a savings cushion.
